blocks.text: Visualising data effectively is crucial for understanding and communicating insights. But how do you choose the right plot and avoid misleading your audience?

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore three fundamental types of data visualisations: histograms, box plots, and scatter plots. Each of these tools serves a different purpose and is suited to different types of data and questions. We will also discuss how to spot misleading features in charts, which is vital for honest data communication.

blocks.title: Histogram
blocks.text: A histogram is a type of bar chart that represents the distribution of numerical data by showing the frequency of data points within certain ranges or 'bins'.

blocks.markdown: Histograms are particularly useful for visualising the distribution of a dataset. The shape of the histogram can provide insights into the underlying distribution, such as whether it is normal, skewed, or bimodal.

blocks.caption: The normal distribution function, often visualised with a histogram.

blocks.title: Interpreting a Histogram
blocks.prompt: Consider a histogram that represents the exam scores of 100 students. The histogram is bell-shaped and symmetric.

steps.text: Identify the shape of the histogram.
steps.latex: The histogram is bell-shaped and symmetric, indicating a normal distribution.

steps.text: Determine what this shape suggests about the data.
steps.latex: A bell-shaped, symmetric histogram suggests that the data is normally distributed, with most scores clustering around the mean.

blocks.answer: The histogram suggests that the exam scores are normally distributed.

blocks.title: Box Plot
blocks.text: A box plot, or box-and-whisker plot, is a graphical representation of data that shows the distribution through quartiles. It highlights the median, upper and lower quartiles, and potential outliers.

blocks.markdown: Box plots are useful for comparing distributions between different groups. They provide a visual summary of the central tendency, variability, and skewness of the data.

blocks.title: Using Box Plots for Comparison
blocks.prompt: You have two datasets representing the heights of plants grown under two different conditions. How can a box plot help compare these datasets?

steps.text: Construct a box plot for each dataset.
steps.latex: The box plot will display the median, quartiles, and potential outliers for each dataset.

steps.text: Compare the medians and interquartile ranges.
steps.latex: The comparison will show differences in central tendency and variability between the two conditions.

blocks.answer: A box plot allows for a visual comparison of the central tendency and spread of the two datasets, highlighting differences in medians and variability.

blocks.title: Scatter Plot
blocks.text: A scatter plot is a type of plot that uses Cartesian coordinates to display values for two variables for a set of data. It is useful for identifying relationships or correlations between the variables.

blocks.markdown: Scatter plots are ideal for visualising the relationship between two continuous variables. Patterns, trends, or correlations can often be observed from the arrangement of the points.

blocks.title: Misleading Charts
blocks.text: Charts can be misleading if they use inappropriate scales, omit data, or distort the visual representation of the data. Always critically evaluate the design of a chart.

blocks.markdown: When creating or interpreting charts, be mindful of potential misrepresentations. Common issues include truncated axes, inconsistent scales, and selective data omission.

points: Histograms are useful for visualising the distribution of numerical data.
Box plots provide a summary of data distribution and are great for comparing groups.
Scatter plots reveal relationships between two continuous variables.
Be aware of misleading features in charts, such as truncated axes or omitted data.
